I know that there have been various projects to do various cryptography related things in Lean in the past - e.g. some of my own work, Joey Lupo's Cryptolib (https://github.com/JoeyLupo/cryptolib/tree/main) and more. I think there's also the work of ArkLib (https://github.com/Verified-zkEVM/ArkLib).

I would like to propose that a library in the vein of mathlib or cslib would be desirable, focused on cryptography - both implementing cryptography and proving things about it. Perhaps this project already exists and I'm not aware of it - but I am not aware of it!

I would like to be involved in such a project but I cannot do it alone - so I would like to ask who IS interested. I think having one repo for cryptography in Lean is desirable compared to many small repos each implementing various things, and having an explictly cryptographic focus is also desirable.

I think any such repo will probably be downstream of mathlib, cslib but I suppose I am willing to hear arguments to the contrary.

A mathlib dependency would be natural, since I expect you'll have good use for groups and related types, right?
Cslib as well, because we're developing languages/frameworks to write and verify sequential and concurrent software. Combining those with crypto primitives would enable, for example, writing and verifying security protocols. Some of the theory in cslib might help with proving crypto primitives correct, too.
Have you considered getting this _into_ cslib?

As the main developer of ArkLib, I definitely agree on having a central cryptolib repo. There are a ton of cryptography to be formalized and much work to set things up - our effort on VCVio is meant to be the base layer for formalization.

Happy to talk more over a call or DM
It might be that it fits better into CSLib, but my feelings is that the concerns of cryptographers are adjacent to but not the same as those of theoretical computer scientists.
Possibly it might be the case that CSLib makes use of it as a dependency.
My sense is that cryptographers are a distinct enough group (separate conferences, separate preprint website) that we should have a separate cryptolib repo as well

I think it'd make good sense, but it'd also be good to keep an eye on what goes where as things develop. For example, some proofs involve defining an operational semantics, which makes cslib or something downstream of it a natural place to carry them out.
I wanna avoid ending up in a circular dependency problem. :-)
Yes definitely.
@Quang Dao who are you aware of who is also doing active work in this area currently?
@Wrenna Robson I use Rocq to formalise my crypto implementation related to electronic voting. (My main goal is to always extract a computer program from my formalisation).
Yeah I'm aware of a lot more work in Rocq in these areas (and in custom tools like EasyCrypt).
The people involved in ArkLib are all I know. There are also some work from the Aeneas team.

Hi, this seems like the best place to ask about my project! Our first idea for my project was to somehow expand on Joey Lupo's library that @Wrenna Robson mentioned, but from looking at VCVio I get the impression that VCVio already is an expansion of the idea of Joey's cryptolib, so I think it makes more sense to use VCVio instead of porting cryptolib to Lean4.
Tagging @Devon Tuma who is the main developer of VCVio. We would love to hear what application you have in mind for the library

I am personally strongly of the view that it would be desirable to both have good, correct, performant, secure implementations of common cryptographic primitives and protocols in Lean, but also link these to both security proofs and proofs of correctness.
There's quite a lot of prior work in this area in Rocq and in more specialised tools like EasyCrypt and many others.
This is why I think performant implementations are particularly of interest to me.

I don't personally work much with the EasyCrypt/Jasmin stack but I work for François Dupressoir who very much does. Trying to get Cameron, who also works for/with him and has done some work with trying to implement EasyCrypt semantics in lean, to come here and share thoughts.

Definitely, all of this is of interest to me & many others. The path toward such a goal is unclear to me however. On the implementation side, I think we should make use of recent tooling (like LeanMLIR) in addition to copying / adapting Jasmin

This is for instance what we are aiming for at ArkLib. At the minimum, have executable spec of SNARK protocols, but moreover, have these spec either be verified to be equivalent to extracted Rust implementation, or, verifiably compile these spec directly to a lower level language (through toolchains like MLIR)

Having had a chat with @Chris Henson today we reckon cryptography can find a home in cslib. I am keen to make this happen, certainly. In the name of getting the ball rolling I want to flag that https://joyofcryptography.com/ might be a good target to start with (in that just as with mathlib starting with undergraduate-level material is probably easier...)
I am aware of at least one person who has said they are formalizing Jonathan Katz’s book. I believe they cover the same ground initially
Well I would encourage them to make PRs to CSLib about it!
I don't know how we want to express statements about probabilistic games
You could define oracles and make queries to them. Like we are doing in Algolean. For probabilistic oracles you could use the PMF monad in their models
Sure. I mean that isn't the only way to do such things but yes
what is algolean?
Of course
It’s my algorithms and complexity library.
Oh no
Why do we have so many libraries covering similar terrain
It’s built on the philosophy that almost all computational models are just query models and algorithms are expressions in a language of combinators on top of them

Wrenna Robson said:

Why do we have so many libraries covering similar terrain

It’s a sad state of affairs. But currently CSLib has severely limited active maintainer capacity outside some areas of CS.

I have had this ambition to build a a grand TCS library for a while now. Thanks to free monads I have decided to push ahead on both the algorithms and complexity theory fronts at Shreyas4991.github.io/Algolean
I think cryptography theory, interactive proofs, zero knowledge proofs etc would be a good fit in algolean (the zkp proof framework of Galois uses the same free monad setup as we do)
I'm inclined to support CSLib through contribution.
Certainly Chris seems very open to it

I am too. But I am currently more focussed on getting my research community on board. I am sure CSLib will sort things out at some point and then we can figure out what CSLib would like from Algolean or not. In any case computer science is too broad and disconnected to fit into one library unlike mathematics.

I am giving a talk about Algolean soon. My idea itself is fairly grand and will at least live on it Algolean. I’ve found institutional backing as well to build a library and already have some researchers on board. More on that in a few months.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Wrenna Robson said:

Why do we have so many libraries covering similar terrain

It’s a sad state of affairs. But currently CSLib has severely limited active maintainer capacity outside some areas of CS.

That's not the issue. The issue is that there's an ongoing technical discussion on potential approaches, and that you raised issues on how this is gonna influence authorship, which we are dealing with (will post an update in the relevant thread soon).

Shreyas Srinivas said:

In any case computer science is too broad and disconnected to fit into one library unlike mathematics.

Also, I guess we'll just keep agreeing to disagree here. ;-)

@Wrenna Robson On the topic of crypto: we'd be very happy to support this in CSLib. Please feel free to open a topic on a possible first step in #CSLib. I also already know of at least one downstream project (CC @Xueying Qin @Marco Peressotti) on distributed protocols based on CSLib that would really benefit from integrating crypto primitives, when they appear.

What I mean is even beyond algorithms we need maintainers in specific areas. For example we now have quantum circuits as a PR in Algolean and I am waiting to get at least one more pair of eyes than mine on it before merging it. We will also soon have NP hardness and completeness notions since expressing reductions is fairly trivial on our model. This is already beginning as a PR. Again we could use an extra maintainer check (though in this case I am technically sufficient).

As far as CS goes we are definitely spread thin as a community.

Hi all, I'm working on formalizing Katz-Lindell with Jon, who is a colleague of mine. For context, Jon and I work on anonymous credentials standards together in the IETF. It is located here: https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/introduction-to-modern-cryptography. What's merged so far is just the simplest stuff, Perfect Secrecy, which you can view here conveniently: https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/introduction-to-modern-cryptography/pull/1.

Would cslib be interested in a PR with that work? The next chapter will likely take some time, as it relies on a definition of PPT which discharging is going to be a PITA in general, because it uses Turing machines. I have techniques for proving time complexity of TMs, but it is still a lot of work. I use Hoare triples augmented with time tracking.
I think the answer is "definitely yes".
That would be a great start.

In the event that cslib ends up msotly cryptography ;) we could consider branching out, but right now I would strongly encourage cryptography PRs into CSLib: they want it, it is a relatively core community library...
Alright, in that case I'll make a PR today with the one time pad and surrounding definitions.
Exciting. I would not call myself a deeply skilled cryptographer but I'm definitely able to review that so tag me in.
Will do :)
Another good source to use as reference for this work might be https://intensecrypto.org/public/index.html, especially because its available online.
Aye. I am happy to point other members of the high assurance cryptography community this way too.
They might have other ideas.

Having a reference is of great help, especially when we add new definitions (or entire areas) to CSLib. It's good to add a reference in the docstring of a new module, if relevant. (Helps with determining if the formalisation is reasonable.)

https://www.hacs-workshop.org/links.html

If anyone isn't familiar with the diversity of cryptography formal methods projects here's a taste
In particular https://www.easycrypt.info/ is a good example of a specialist theorem prove in this area

I would imagine it might be also be possible to use some of the work of SSProve (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3594735) in some way. Certainly the point is we're not starting from scratch here - even if some stuff must be done in "the Lean way"

I've done substantially more on the crypto side in my personal fork of cslib, but its much, much more code and it is all partially reviewed so I am not planning on upstreaming it in its current shape.

In particular, I proved the security of Fiat-Shamir against PPT adversaries given the underlying relation game is secure against PPT adversaries.
Nice.
There are some ideas in there that I would be interested in upstreaming more slowly though.

Essentially while I am not a CSLib maintainer of any kind, I would say that I'm keen to encourage fellow community members to contribute, working with the maintainers to make the review load for them manageable.
My suspicion is that a lot of people have work of this and that form in private or obscure repos and it would be great to pull things together, but that's necessarily a slow process I think
Well I think also with https://github.com/Verified-zkEVM/VCV-io and https://github.com/Verified-zkEVM/ArkLib there's already two reasonable starts!
Well indeed :)
But integrating that stuff into CSLib would be even better.

I'm personally not totally sure what does and doesn't belong in cslib on the cryptography side, but this particularly simple thing at least seems quite sane to add. Made a PR here: https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/464

So for a long time I wasn't sure. I think essentially we will be better served by getting as much in as possible. If down the road it would be more appropriate to have a "cryptolib" proper that's all for the good, but I have been reflecting on how much Mathlib's strength was in non-pickiness with these things.

I think there's lots of value in having crypto sitting in the same lib as other topics. Concurrency models, algorithms, and logics come to mind as immediate synergies. So I appreciate the push towards integration.
I think one of the maintainers ought to enable CI on this PR. Since this is Samuel’s first CSLib PR CI won’t run automatically
I've clicked the button, should be running.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

What I mean is even beyond algorithms we need maintainers in specific areas.

This was also true of mathlib when it was a small project -- it started with two maintainers, neither of whom were professional mathematicians. What made it a success was continual PRs to the repo from the community and then people _wanted_ to be maintainers in order to make the library grow. It is also the case that mathematics is extremely disparate and it's surprising but true that we have one mathematics library which is able to capture a very large part of pure mathematics.
@Kevin Buzzard : Math had bourbaki almost a century ago at this point. We haven’t had anything similar in CS since the field only came into proper existence after the 1950s
Well, let there be a Bourbakist of bits

Wrenna Robson said:

Having had a chat with Chris Henson today we reckon cryptography can find a home in cslib. I am keen to make this happen, certainly. In the name of getting the ball rolling I want to flag that https://joyofcryptography.com/ might be a good target to start with (in that just as with mathlib starting with undergraduate-level material is probably easier...)

My BSc thesis includes the formalisation of the first two chapters (of the old edition) and (technically to be completed) the ElGamal security proof, using VCVio as a base. Happy to discuss this further!
Super. PR it :). Let's build a foundation.

I've also done a crypto formalization during my bachelor thesis - specifically Elligator: Elliptic-curve points indistinguishable from uniform random strings.
Not sure if this is too specialized for the beginning stage in CSLib?

At the moment, I'm working on improving the overall code quality (this was my first Lean project) before opening a PR if any interest exists.
If you are working on elliptic curves, you might want to get some of the basic theory into mathlib

Shreyas Srinivas said:

If you are working on elliptic curves, you might want to get some of the basic theory into mathlib

There are indeed some parts which might be more properly placed there. I had to define my own Legendre symbol + some concrete field property helper lemmas. However I'm not a real algebraist who would know if these are indeed most generally defined from a mathematicians point of view. I will leave this discussion for the actual PR.
@Kevin Buzzard : Is elliptic curve theory interesting in FLT? I have no clue about it but I heard you talk about elliptic curves at some point in connection with FLT

Yes it is, but doing ECC is way more concrete w.r.t. to specific fields and about which aspects you care about if compared to the general theory behind it. I wouldn't consider my work to be of particular interested regarding the general theory of elliptic curves (not to mention FLT).

But I'm sure @Kevin Buzzard is way more knowledgable regarding the big picture and what mathlib is lacking or not.
Surprisingly, you do not need much of a ECC basis to prove the linked paper. I mostly utilized standard finite field theory already given in mathlib.
Yes, elliptic curves are a key ingredient in FLT, and we have a bunch of the theory already in mathlib: docs#EllipticCurve .
We also have Legendre symbols -- see e.g. https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/NumberTheory/LegendreSymbol/QuadraticReciprocity.html

Kevin Buzzard said:

Yes, elliptic curves are a key ingredient in FLT, and we have a bunch of the theory already in mathlib: docs#EllipticCurve .

that's a 404 for me
@Chris Anto Fröschl : In this case, I think your PR should try to build on the mathlib definitions. This might definitely entail some work, but we try to harmonise definitions where we can

Kevin Buzzard said:

We also have Legendre symbols -- see e.g. https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/NumberTheory/LegendreSymbol/QuadraticReciprocity.html

Yes I knew about that. However, the paper uses a Legendre symbol which is extendable to prime powers (not just primes). Therefore resulting in other properties.

I don't think there exists a general abstraction to catch both cases without losing any properties of the other (?)
Maybe it's time for a separate Elliptic curves thread.

Aside : There is a docstring mismatch between the statement and docstring of the quadratic reciprocity theorem : https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/NumberTheory/LegendreSymbol/QuadraticReciprocity.html#legendreSym.quadratic_reciprocity

For anyone interested in the meantime, my formalization is at http://src.2718281828.de/elligator/
There is also a slightly outdated blueprint doc at https://chrisathmedu.github.io/elligator/docs/Elligator.html

I will open a PR as soon as I find the time.
You mean this legendre symbol? http://src.2718281828.de/elligator/tree/Elligator/LegendreSymbol.lean?h=main#n14 ?
Yes. Although this might generalize a bit more as soon as I get a chance to implement Elligator 2 (which loosens some of the restrictions associated w.r.t. the order q)

Or perhaps eventually a cryptography topic as we do have much to discuss.

Excuse me being imprecise. I didn't expect going much beyond a little announcement regarding the potential PR. The actual paper definition (formalized def):

This however is later in Elligator 2 (other context for more potential curve candidates) extended to odd prime power orders (currently not formalized):

I didn't use the Jacobi symbol because it is restricted toInt -> Int. However thinking about it, I could have perhaps made this just a wrapper def, casting the result of the existing jacobiSym to a field element while maintaining the remaining field properties depending on context, thereby creating a F_q -> F_q version.
I'm not sure if this is the most elegant solution or even a generally viable cast inside the def, but I will give it a try. Nevertheless, I would only be able to base my actual Legendre symbol def on the jacobiSym like this. Therefore, the actual API of my formalization still depending on my 'custom' Legendre symbol wrapper. @Kevin Buzzard did I miss something obvious?

We can also move the discussion regarding Elligator back into the long forgotten original thread to avoid further digress of the main topic.
Yes this is not the Jacobi symbol. A general element of Fq\mathbb{F}_qFq​ cannot be represented by an integer so this is something else.

Would you then consider this to be of any use in mathlib? It seems kinda context bound w.r.t. to this paper and therefore is perhaps best kept anywhere close to the rest of the formalization, i.e. inside CSLib (?).
Otherwise, this would rather deserve the maximum viable generalization.

For q odd this is nothing more than x↦x(q−1)/2x\mapsto x^{(q-1)/2}x↦x(q−1)/2 and in contrast to the Legendre symbol (where there are amazing relationships between (p/q)(p/q)(p/q) and (q/p)(q/p)(q/p) I'm not sure that there are any amazing relationships here.
